body_markdown:
A car’s design creates your first impression of it, but its dashboard is what you live with, day in and day out. It needs to do *something* well—it has to be attractive, or practical and easy to use, or an ideal combination of both.


Glitz or simplicity, screens or ’80s digital or old-school dials, we all have a preference. Here are five of our favorites, just to get the conversation started. Let us know yours in the comments.


## Digital vs. Analog


Wikimedia Commons/Dave_7


I truly love the digital dashboard in my 1985 Corvette, but as cool as the pixels are, I would much prefer the warmth of wood and the sweep of mechanical needles. Plenty of cars have that, but only a few manage to put the right amount of flair on top of the functionality.


Buick got it just right in the early 1940s with a simple three-gauge layout backed by an engine-turned panel. It gives just enough flair to be visually interesting without being too much. A matching clock sits directly in front of the passenger, and the radio controls tuck slightly lower. It’s uncluttered, simple, and conveys everything the driver needs. — *Kyle Smith*


## C2 Corvette


Mecum Auctions


I was going to share my favorite dashboard of my youth, the one in the Bandit-era Trans Am, but Kyle picked a car with a much more elegant engine-turned finish. With that, the C2 Corvette gets my nod. The dual-cowl look and perfectly placed gauges (and the vertical radio) yield a perfect blend of beauty and purpose. Just staring at this dash feels like an event. — *Eddy Eckart*


## Boomerang!


Instagram/lambolog/Kaan Yener


I also love the digital dash in Kyle’s Corvette (and the slightly less digital one in my old ’94 Corvette). “Best” is subjective here, but Giugiaro’s[Maserati Boomerang](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/maserati-boomerang-concept/) concept car from 1971–72 certainly gets the job done. While the Boomerang’s body gets a lot of credit for kicking off the wedge-shaped craze of the ’70s, its interior was just as wild, just not as influential. It packs almost all the gauges (tach, battery, fuel, oil pressure, oil temp, water temp, but no speedo for some reason) and controls (turn signal, lights) immediately ahead of the driver. The steering wheel just sort of wraps around that panel and connects to the steering column behind it. Speaking of the steering column, it is apparently a “divided steering column connected by a chain,” according to Italdesign, though I can’t find exactly how it works. — *Andrew Newton*


## Simplicity, With Screens and Without


Honda


Road trips in my ’86 Volvo 240 impressed upon me the delightful calm of a screen-free interior, but as a child of the ’90s, with several long-distance close friends, I’ll admit it: I really do love a well-executed—and appropriately sized—digital screen in my daily driver. The setup of the current Honda Civic Si is just what I’m looking for, in a car I might realistically purchase: Clearly legible, crisp displays with no artsy flourishes, real buttons on the steering wheel plus actual knobs for HVAC, and clean lines with materials that read nicer than they are.


That said, I would love to experience the maximalist steampunk aesthetic that is a Pagani interior, even if I couldn’t actually drive the car. — *Grace Jarvis*


## Engine-Turned…All the Way


Flickr/Paul Williams


I have always loved the look of engine-turned dashboards. I think I first discovered them on old Bugattis and thought they were so cool. But my all-time favorite dash, which is part of probably the best interior of all time, is in the Spyker C8. The blend of dials and toggles on that machined aluminum—all of it framed by leather—is just gorgeous. — *Stefan Lombard*
